name: Plakas v. Drinski
court: Seventh Circuit (from a federal district court in Indiana)
topic: Fourth Amendment deadly force; man with a fireplace poker charging a deputy; no constitutional duty to use less deadly alternatives first; no constitutional duty to equip or train for every alternative
summary: A handcuffed, intoxicated arrestee escaped, armed himself with a fireplace poker, struck an officer, fled into the woods, refused a half hour of persuasion to surrender, told a deputy that one of them would die there, and then charged the deputy with the poker raised. The deputy shot him once and killed him. The Seventh Circuit affirmed summary judgment, holding that the Fourth Amendment does not require officers to use the least deadly or even a less deadly alternative when deadly force is otherwise reasonable, and that the Constitution does not require a county to supply particular equipment or train officers to use every alternative. The court analyzed the encounter in segments and judged the shooting from the moment of the charge forward. It is taught as the deadly force statement of the no least intrusive alternative rule, with the caution that Barnes v. Felix later rejected any rule confining the inquiry to the moment of the threat.
coverage: The full opinion by Judge Zagel (District Judge, sitting by designation, with Circuit Judges Cummings and Coffey), including all footnotes, was read from the Public.Resource.Org Federal Reporter archive at https://law.resource.org/pub/us/case/reporter/F3/019/19.F3d.1143.93-1431.html. The archive file is headed 19 F.3d 1143, No. 93-1431, argued November 1, 1993, decided March 21, 1994, which confirms the citation.

The archive text has paragraph numbers but no Federal Reporter page breaks, so no pin cites are given. The Sixth Circuit in Hart v. City of Grand Rapids (read for a companion brief) quotes Plakas's segment analysis language and attributes it to page 1150.
The district court opinion (811 F. Supp. 1356) was not read. The opinion does not name the district; Newton County, Indiana, where the events occurred, is described only as the court described it.

Course materials teach Plakas for the proposition that officers need not use less deadly alternatives. That matches the holding. The brief adds, as the assignment requested, that the court's segmented analysis judged the shooting from the moment of the charge forward and declined to revisit prior segments, and that the Supreme Court in Barnes v. Felix (2025) rejected any rule that precludes consideration of prior events, while leaving open the officer created danger question that Plakas addressed through Carter v. Buscher.
facts:
The facts are as the Seventh Circuit recited them, adopting the version most favorable to the plaintiff. At about 9:30 p.m. on February 2, 1991, Konstantino Plakas was found walking along a state road in Newton County, Indiana, after his car had rolled into a water filled ditch. A paramedic drove him back to the scene, where he refused medical treatment. He smelled of alcohol, had difficulty communicating, and agreed to go to the sheriff's department for an intoxication test. Corporal Koby frisked and handcuffed him behind his back. Plakas complained that cuffing behind his back hurt because of burn scars on his chest; Koby said it was department policy. Plakas got into the squad car voluntarily, but as Koby drove away Plakas opened the rear door, which still had its handle, and fled into snow covered woods still handcuffed.

Plakas ran to the home of the family of his fiancée, where he fell face first through the doorway. He told them he had wrecked his car and that his head hurt. The father, Roy Ailes, told him not to run from police and went out to tell officers Plakas was there and willing to come out. When Koby and the paramedic entered, Plakas, who had worked his cuffed hands to the front of his body, became loud and combative. He backed into a corner, picked up a two to three foot fireplace poker with a hook on the end, screamed, rushed Koby, and struck Koby's wrist with the poker, then chased Koby away as he tried to reenter through another door. Plakas slammed the poker into a wall and beat his head against the wall.

Plakas walked out the front door. Deputy Jeffrey Drinski and State Trooper Perras followed with guns drawn. Roy Ailes ran forward saying not to shoot and tried to talk Plakas into surrendering. The officers told Plakas to drop the poker. He lowered it but did not lay it down, raised it but did not swing, then turned, tripped over a wire fence, and ran into the woods with the poker. The officers chased him to a small clearing in thick brush. Plakas turned and faced Drinski and Perras from about ten feet away; Sergeant King stood outside the clearing. Drinski blocked the opening the men had come through.

For the next quarter to half hour Drinski and Perras tried to talk Plakas into surrendering, telling him people cared about him and nobody needed to get hurt, and telling him to drop the weapon and get on the ground. Plakas opened his shirt to show his scars. King thought Drinski might succeed; Drinski did not believe Plakas was ever ready to surrender. Plakas pointed the poker at Drinski and said, in substance, either you are going to die here or I am going to die here, and told him to go ahead and shoot because his life was not worth anything. He repeated these thoughts often. Then Plakas tried to break through the brush, turned back to Drinski, who was 12 to 15 feet away, raised the poker, and charged. Drinski backed away until something, a tree or a stumble, stopped his retreat. He saw Plakas cock the poker over his head for a swing and, when Plakas was two arm lengths away, fired once at his chest. Plakas died at the hospital.

Drinski feared for his life; Perras testified he would have shot if Drinski had not. Perras had a canister of chemical repellant on his belt that could have disabled Plakas, a canine unit had been offered about ten minutes earlier, and the officers could have tried to keep barriers and distance between themselves and Plakas. Plakas's administrator sued Drinski and Newton County under section 1983. The district court granted summary judgment.
holding:
Affirmed.

Self defense under Garner and Graham. This was not an escape case but a self defense case in which the officer had probable cause to believe the suspect posed a significant threat of death or serious physical injury. Drinski faced a man who minutes earlier had attacked an officer with a dangerous weapon, had refused several entreaties to disarm, had said one of the two would die that night, and then moved toward him raising the weapon to strike. Shooting a man who has told you he is going to use deadly force against you and then moves toward you as if to do so is unquestionably an act of self defense, even if, as the plaintiff's expert maintained, the man was attempting suicide by police.

Scrutiny of the officer's account. The court said summary judgment in deadly force cases must be granted with particular care where the officer is the only surviving witness, because the only person likely to contradict him is beyond reach; a court must critically assess the forensic evidence, the officer's original statements, and expert opinion. Here that principle did not fit well: a non defendant trooper from another agency corroborated Drinski, and the discrepancies the plaintiff raised (the position of the body, which had been moved, and whether a tree or a sapling stopped Drinski's retreat) were not enough to let a rational factfinder decide against him.

Provocation theory rejected on the facts. The argument that self defense is unavailable to an officer whose own brutality provoked the attack failed because the inference that Koby beat Plakas could not reasonably be drawn and because, even if he had, Koby was not at the scene of the shooting. Drinski did not cause Plakas to attack him.

No duty to use alternatives. Taken literally the argument failed because Drinski did use alternatives: he talked for a long time and tried to retreat. As to the broader claim, there was no precedent in any circuit holding that the Constitution requires officers to use all feasible alternatives to avoid a situation where deadly force can justifiably be used. Ford v. Childers refused to require a warning shot; Carter v. Buscher rejected the proposition that the Fourth Amendment prohibits creating unreasonably dangerous circumstances in which to effect a legal arrest. "The Fourth Amendment does not require officers to use the least intrusive or even less intrusive alternatives in search and seizure cases. The only test is whether what the police officers actually did was reasonable." The court did not believe the Fourth Amendment requires the use of the least or even a less deadly alternative so long as the use of deadly force is reasonable under Garner and Graham. Tom v. Voida did not announce a duty to consider all alternatives; it described an officer's quick decision to draw her firearm rather than reach for chemical spray.

The time frame and the segments. The court said the decision to shoot can only be made after the briefest reflection and asked whether Drinski, as Plakas moved toward him, was supposed to think of an attack dog, the trooper's gas, or how fast he could run backwards; its answer was no, because there is too little time and too much opportunity to second guess. It explained that every force case begins with an officer's decision to do something and that the officer in that sense always causes the trouble, but it is trouble the officer is sworn to cause. "So we carve up the incident into segments and judge each on its own terms to see if the officer was reasonable at each stage." Each prior step here, the arrest, the pursuit of the escapee, drawing weapons after Plakas armed himself and attacked, following him into the clearing, and trying to talk him down, was reasonable, so Drinski was properly standing in the clearing with his gun when Plakas charged. "It is from that point on that we judge the reasonableness of the use of deadly force in light of all that the officer knew. We do not return to the prior segments of the event and, in light of hindsight, reconsider whether the prior police decisions were correct." The court added that it does consider the whole of the event as it appears to the officer, and concluded that the undisputed facts led to one conclusion: Drinski's use of deadly force was reasonable given Plakas's act of aggression and Drinski's knowledge of what had gone before.

Equipment and training. No precedent holds that a governmental unit has a constitutional duty to supply particular equipment, and the Fifth Circuit had held the Constitution does not require agencies to maintain equipment useful in all foreseeable situations. The court declined to let juries hear that an arrestee would have been uninjured if only the police had disabling gas, a capture net, a taser, or more officers and then find a municipality liable for failing to buy them: "the Constitution does not enact a police administrator's equipment list." It likewise declined to impose a constitutional requirement to train police to use all available equipment beyond the acceptable training program already mandated, noting the plaintiff's expert's opinion that Drinski might have been better trained to negotiate but that no one contended any misstatement caused the charge.
notDecided:
Whether an officer whose own unjustified force provoked an attack may claim self defense. The court distinguished the Eleventh Circuit's Gilmere decision on the facts and said it neither approved nor disapproved its holding.

Whether the trooper's failure to use his chemical repellant was reasonable. The court said that inaction could not be attributed to Drinski or Newton County because the trooper was not a defendant and not under the county's command.

Whether state law imposes a duty to retreat or to use alternatives. The court noted that state law rules might exist but do not impose constitutional duties, citing Reed v. Hoy.

What an adequate training program requires. The court referred to the acceptable training program already mandated and declined to add a constitutional requirement to train on every piece of equipment; it did not define the baseline.

How earlier events bear on reasonableness when they are relevant. The court said it considers the whole event as it appears to the officer but refused to reconsider prior decisions with hindsight. The Supreme Court's later decision in Barnes v. Felix holds that the totality inquiry has no time limit and that no rule may preclude consideration of prior events, while reserving whether or how an officer's own creation of a dangerous situation factors in.
inPractice:
Plakas is the deadly force version of a rule officers hear in every force class: the Fourth Amendment asks whether what you did was reasonable, not whether something less deadly was available. The Seventh Circuit put it directly. When a man who has struck an officer with a poker, refused a half hour of negotiation, announced that one of you will die, and then charges with the weapon raised is two arm lengths away, the officer is not required to think about the dog that was offered ten minutes ago, the trooper's chemical spray, or how fast he can run backwards. The decision to shoot is made in an instant, and the court refused to second guess it.

The case also protects agencies on a point instructors should know. There is no constitutional duty to buy particular equipment or to train officers on every alternative. An expert's testimony that a taser, a net, or a dog would have produced a better result does not make the county liable. That is a federal constitutional rule; it does not displace state training mandates, department policy, or the agency's own judgment about what to field.

Two cautions. First, Plakas is often summarized as saying the court looked only at the moment of the charge. The court did say it judges the shooting from that point on and will not revisit earlier decisions with hindsight, and it drew that approach from the officer created danger cases. In Barnes v. Felix (2025) the Supreme Court held that the totality of the circumstances inquiry has no time limit and that no rule may exclude prior events from the analysis, while expressly leaving the officer created danger question open. Plakas's no alternatives holding survives Barnes; its language about not returning to prior segments must now be read in light of Barnes. In Plakas itself the earlier events all favored the deputy, and Barnes says such context counts.

Second, Dr. Sowards pairs Plakas with Scott v. Henrich as the no least intrusive alternative pair and reminds California officers that state law and policy since 2019 ask them to consider feasible alternatives and de escalation. Drinski did exactly that for half an hour before he had to shoot; the record of that effort is why the court found his account credible.
trainIt:
Teach the half hour before the shot. Drinski talked, kept distance, tried to retreat, and had another officer and a sergeant positioned. The court held he did not have to use the other alternatives, but his effort is what made the final decision easy to defend. Use the clearing as a scenario: an armed, intoxicated, possibly suicidal man ten to fifteen feet away, a hedge for a barrier, a canine offered, a partner with chemical spray. Have students plan containment, communication, and less lethal options while maintaining a deadly force response, and then have them articulate the point at which the plan ended and why. Students should state that the law did not require any of the alternatives and that good practice called for all of them that time allowed.

Teach the segmented analysis with Barnes in hand. Walk the segments the court identified: the arrest, the pursuit, drawing weapons after the poker attack, entering the clearing, the negotiation, the charge. Plakas judged each segment on its own terms and then judged the shooting from the charge forward. Barnes v. Felix now requires that the whole timeline be available to a court reviewing the final decision. In Plakas every earlier segment supported the deputy; students should see that under Barnes those facts, the attack on Koby, the threats, the refusal to disarm, are exactly what makes the shooting reasonable.

Teach the suicide by police point. The court said the man's apparent wish to be shot did not change the analysis. Train students to recognize that pattern, to use time and communication when they have it, and to understand that it does not require them to absorb a blow from a raised weapon.

Teach the equipment and training holding to instructors and supervisors as a federal floor, not a ceiling. The Constitution does not require a particular tool or a particular class. State mandates and department policy do, and an agency that fields a tool must train it.
caution: Read in full from the Public.Resource.Org archive without reporter page breaks, so no pin cites are given. The opinion was written by a district judge sitting by designation for a Seventh Circuit panel and is binding in the Seventh Circuit, not the Ninth. The no alternatives and equipment holdings remain intact, but the court's statement that it judges the shooting from the moment of the charge forward and does not return to prior segments must be read in light of Barnes v. Felix, 605 U.S. 73 (2025), which rejected any rule that precludes consideration of prior events in the totality of the circumstances while leaving the officer created danger question open. The facts were adopted in the plaintiff's favor on summary judgment, with the deputy's account corroborated by a non defendant trooper.

applications.title: No duty to use a less deadly alternative
applications.body: Where deadly force is otherwise reasonable under Garner and Graham, the Fourth Amendment does not require the officer to use the least deadly or even a less deadly option first. The only test is whether what the officer actually did was reasonable.

applications.title: The instant of decision
applications.body: The court refused to require an officer facing a charging man with a raised weapon to think about a dog, chemical spray, or retreat. The decision to shoot is made after the briefest reflection, and courts will not second guess it when the threat is clear.

applications.title: Alternatives were used anyway
applications.body: Drinski talked for up to half an hour, kept distance, and tried to retreat. The court noted he did use alternatives before shooting. That record is why the account was credible and why the plaintiff's theories failed.

applications.title: No constitutional equipment list
applications.body: A county has no constitutional duty to supply particular equipment or to train on every alternative. Expert testimony that a taser, net, or dog would have helped does not create municipal liability under section 1983.

applications.title: Read the segment analysis with Barnes
applications.body: Plakas judged the shooting from the moment of the charge forward and declined to revisit earlier segments. Barnes v. Felix (2025) holds that the totality inquiry has no time limit and that prior events cannot be excluded by rule. The no alternatives holding stands; the timing language does not.

quiz.q: What did the Seventh Circuit hold about an officer's duty to use alternatives before deadly force in Plakas v. Drinski?
options: Officers must try every available less lethal option first
Officers must fire a warning shot
The Fourth Amendment does not require the least or even a less deadly alternative so long as the use of deadly force is reasonable under Garner and Graham
Officers must wait for a canine unit if one is available
quiz.teach: The court found no precedent requiring officers to use all feasible alternatives and said the only test is whether what the officers actually did was reasonable.

quiz.q: What did the court say about the county's obligation to provide equipment such as chemical spray, a taser, or a canine?
options: The county was liable for failing to provide them
There is no constitutional duty to supply particular equipment; the Constitution does not enact a police administrator's equipment list
The county had to prove the equipment was unavailable
The question was sent to a jury
quiz.teach: The court declined to let juries find municipalities liable on expert testimony that a different tool would have avoided injury, and declined to impose a constitutional duty to train on all available equipment.

quiz.q: How should Plakas's statement that the court judges the shooting from the moment of the charge forward be read today?
options: As the controlling rule for all deadly force cases

In light of Barnes v. Felix, which held that the totality of the circumstances inquiry has no time limit and that prior events cannot be excluded by rule, while leaving the officer created danger question open
quiz.teach: Plakas's holding that no less deadly alternative is required survives. Its segmented, moment forward framing must be read with Barnes, which requires courts to consider the events leading up to the force.
